whatTheyArgued: Dignaga (Pramanasamuccaya) founded the Buddhist apoha theory: words convey meaning through exclusion of what is other, and he rejected universals as referents. Our snip (Stcherbatsky 1930, Jinendrabuddhi's summary of Pram.-samuc.-vrtti ad V.11) says the meaning of a word consists in repudiating the discrepant meaning. He also accepted only perception and inference as pramanas and gave the three-aspect test for a valid reason (trairupya). Nothing in his work, as I read it, treats a claim as a hypothesis with counted support.

scholarship.ref: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epistemology in Classical Indian Philosophy'
scholarship.supports: perception and inference only; apoha; trairupya as three conditions on a reason
scholarship.disputes: Later logicians (Dharmakirti, Uddyotakara) reinterpreted apoha causally and modified the reason conditions; scholars disagree whether apoha is merely negative. I only read a summary of this and a search snippet on apoha.

ourUse: asserted.js: a relation edge's verb is a hypothesis with counted support (witnesses by recurrence, seeded shuffled-copy counts); standing 'corroborated' at 2 witnesses, never a verdict.

bends.ours: Compendium: 'A claim is a hypothesis whose support is counted, never a recovered fact.'
bends.theirs: Not found in Dignaga or the scholarship read. His inference theory requires three conditions on the reason, which is a logical test, not a count of witnesses.

bends.ours: 'a word designates by excluding its contraries' as warrant for the verb-hypothesis tier.
bends.theirs: Apoha is a semantic theory of conceptual content over universals; asserted.js excludes nothing semantically and its mechanism (recurrence, shuffle nulls) is unrelated.
It is Jinendrabuddhi's summary quoting the vrtti, in Stcherbatsky's translation, with OCR line breaks; disclosed, not Dignaga's own text in his own wording.

bends.theirs: Model-generated text in the author's voice; Dignaga said nothing about rigidity or nuance.
